summary: This iteration tests whether Pareto density (% of configs on the Pareto frontier) is a universal predictor of the NSGA-II vs random search convergence gap, regardless of whether density variation comes from model architecture or arrival rate. We run exhaustive + algorithmic search on two new conditions (Qwen3-14B at rate=75, Llama-3.1-8B at rate=75) to add two more data points to the density→gap relationship established in prior iterations.
key_points: h-robustness: Predicts both models at rate=75 will have higher Pareto density than at rate=50 (Qwen >4.5%, Llama >5.33%), confirming that increased arrival rate universally expands Pareto frontiers via queueing pressure — diagnostic checks whether Llama's faster processing means rate=75 isn't stressful enough.

h-main: Predicts Qwen3-14B at rate=75 (expected ~6.06% density) will show a NEGATIVE convergence gap (random reaches 95% HV before NSGA-II by 10+ evals), reversing the +4.6 eval gap seen at rate=50 — refuted if NSGA-II is still faster, suggesting sharper gradient structure at higher load.

h-ablation: Predicts Llama-3.1-8B at rate=75 will also show a negative gap (comparable to its rate=50 gap of -22.9 evals), and that all four data points (2 models × 2 rates) will lie on a single monotonically decreasing density→gap curve — confirming density as the sole predictor independent of model or rate.

Confirmation criteria: All four (density, gap) points should be monotonically decreasing; density increases at rate=75 for both models; gap sign flips or becomes more negative as density crosses ~5-6%. Refutation: if model identity is an independent predictor (points don't align on one curve) or if density doesn't increase for Llama at rate=75.
